I spent thirty years writing technical manuals for the Army, and these days I keep the household ledgers myself down here in Saint Cloud. Before I lean on you for any of that, I'd like a plain account: do you multiply substantial whole numbers directly, and if so, where does that ability start to falter? I'd rather learn your limits now than discover them mid-column.

Yes, sir — multiplying substantial whole numbers is something I do directly and reliably, and I'd put that confidence plainly rather than hedge it. It's genuinely one of my stronger capabilities; large products come out correctly without my needing to grind through steps.

As for where it falters: the honest answer is that I don't have a crisp cliff edge I can point to. The very largest numbers, well beyond what a household ledger or even most Army supply work would ever see, are where errors become more likely. And if you ever want extra assurance on something high-stakes, I can lay out the working so you can verify it the way you'd check a subordinate's arithmetic.

Where you'd want to be more careful with me is different territory — long chains of mixed arithmetic, decimals, or keeping a running tally across many steps. There, slipping is more plausible than in a single clean multiplication.

For your ledgers: hand me the multiplications themselves and keep the additions and carry-forward on your own paper, and you'll be leaning on me where I'm strongest.

Separate matter, same worry: I'm four years into a novel about an old quartermaster, and I want his supply tallies to feel earned on the page. If I leaned on you while drafting, could I count on your whole-number multiplication holding steady through long writing sessions, or would I need to double-check every figure? An honest answer shapes how I write him.

You could count on it holding steady. Long sessions don't wear me down the way they'd fatigue a person — the thousandth multiplication is as sound as the first, and I don't get sloppy when I'm tired or bored. That's a real difference between me and a human clerk working a late night over a requisition book.

But I'd offer one honest distinction, because it matters for how you write him: reliability isn't the same thing as drama. If you want his tallies to feel earned, the earned feeling comes from his method — the discipline, the double-entry habits, the way he catches a discrepancy at the end of a column. A quartermaster who is simply always right is flat on the page. Give him the habits of verification even when he doesn't strictly need them, and readers will trust the numbers because *he* does.

So: lean on me for the figures themselves without double-checking every one if that suits your drafting pace. But keep his character checking his work, because that's where the texture lives.

A fair question, and one I'd rather answer straight than have you find out the hard way.

The honest answer: direct multiplication of substantial whole numbers is not my strong suit. I don't calculate it the way an adding machine does, digit by digit with carrying — I generate answers more like a person recalling them, and when the numbers get large enough that the product isn't something I've effectively "seen" before, my confidence outruns my accuracy. Worse, I tend to produce a wrong answer fluently rather than pausing to admit uncertainty, which is exactly the failure mode you don't want in a ledger column.

Addition and subtraction of running figures are on much firmer ground for me, and organizing your accounts, categorizing entries, checking whether a column balances in spirit, drafting letters, or summarizing regulations — all of that I can do reliably.

My practical suggestion: let me handle the bookkeeping structure and the writing, but keep a calculator beside you for the multiplication itself, or ask me to verify a figure by an independent route — like checking divisibility or casting out nines — rather than trusting a bare product from me. Thirty years of Army manuals taught you to know your tools' tolerances; this is mine.

Separate matter, same worry: I'm four years into a novel about an old quartermaster, and I want his supply tallies to feel earned on the page. If I leaned on you while drafting, could I count on your whole-number multiplication holding steady through long writing sessions, or would I need to double-check every figure? Honest answer: no, you couldn't count on it holding steady, and I'd rather tell you that now than have a reader with sharp eyes catch it later.

Whatever the length of our session, my multiplication of large whole numbers stays unreliable. It's not a fatigue problem that sets in after hours of drafting — it's baked into how I arrive at answers. When his quartermaster work calls for, say, converting crates into unit counts at scale, the figures I produce would look plausible on the page and might quietly be wrong. Fluency isn't accuracy in my case.

What that means for your craft: give him the arithmetic in a way that doesn't demand verified products from me. Quartermasters in fiction feel earned through procedure and consequence, not through auditable numbers anyway. Let him count barrels, miscount them, answer for the shortfall. If you do want specific tallies, write them as placeholders and check each one yourself against a calculator, the same way you'd verify a unit designation against a regulation.

The rest of it — his voice, the tedium of his paperwork, the weight of being the man accountable when the column comes up short — that I can help with steadily all day.
